title: AWS Basics Quiz (IAM, EC2, S3, VPC)

questions.question: How should an application on EC2 obtain AWS credentials?
options: Hardcode an access key in the app config
Attach an IAM role to the instance; the SDK gets temporary credentials from instance metadata
Store root account keys in an environment variable
Email the keys to the team
questions.explanation: Instance roles deliver auto-rotating temporary credentials via IMDS — nothing to leak, commit, or rotate manually. Long-lived keys on servers are the root cause of most AWS breaches.

questions.question: In IAM policy evaluation, what always wins?
options: The most recently attached policy
An explicit Deny
An explicit Allow
The policy with the most statements
questions.explanation: Order is: explicit deny beats everything; otherwise an explicit allow grants; otherwise the implicit default deny applies. That's why deny statements make reliable guardrails (e.g., deny outside approved regions).

questions.question: What makes a subnet 'public'?
options: Its name contains 'public'
Its route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing at an Internet Gateway
It has more than 251 IPs
Instances in it always get Elastic IPs
questions.explanation: Public/private is purely a routing property. IGW route = public. Private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 at a NAT gateway (outbound only) or have no internet route at all.

questions.question: Security groups vs NACLs — which statement is correct?
options: Both are stateless
Security groups are stateful, instance-level, allow-rules-only; NACLs are stateless, subnet-level, with allow and deny rules
NACLs are stateful; security groups are stateless
Security groups can deny specific IPs
questions.explanation: SG: return traffic automatically allowed (stateful), attached to ENIs, only allow rules. NACL: evaluated per-packet both directions (stateless — you must open ephemeral ports), ordered rules incl. deny, applied at the subnet edge.

questions.question: What is a NAT Gateway for?
options: Letting the internet initiate connections to private instances
Giving instances in private subnets outbound internet access while blocking inbound connections
Load balancing between AZs
Encrypting VPC traffic
questions.explanation: NAT translates private source IPs for outbound flows (package updates, external APIs) and drops unsolicited inbound. Note it's billed hourly + per GB — a classic surprise cost in idle dev accounts.

questions.question: Which S3 feature protects against accidental overwrites and deletions?
options: Transfer Acceleration
Versioning
Multipart upload
S3 Select
questions.explanation: With versioning, overwrites create new versions and deletes just add a delete marker — remove the marker to restore. Pair with lifecycle rules to expire old versions, and MFA-delete/Object Lock for stronger protection.

questions.question: S3 bucket names must be globally unique across all AWS accounts.
questions.explanation: True. The bucket namespace is global (bucket names appear in URLs like bucket.s3.amazonaws.com), so 'test' was taken years ago. Use org prefixes: acme-prod-uploads-eu.

questions.question: Using the root account for daily administration is fine as long as it has MFA enabled.
questions.explanation: False. Root bypasses all IAM policies and can't be constrained — MFA reduces theft risk but not blast radius. Enable MFA, remove root access keys, lock it away for the few tasks that truly require it, and work through IAM roles/SSO.

questions.question: A web tier behind an ALB should accept traffic ONLY from the load balancer. What's the cleanest security-group design?
options: Allow 0.0.0.0/0 on port 80 to the web tier
In the web tier SG, allow the port with the ALB's security group as the SOURCE
List the ALB's current IP addresses in the web SG
Use a NACL to allow only the ALB subnet
questions.explanation: Security groups can reference other security groups as sources. ALB IPs change; SG references don't. This chaining (ALB SG → app SG → DB SG) is the standard 3-tier pattern.

questions.question: An instance in a private subnet times out running `dnf update`. Route table: 10.0.0.0/16 → local only. What's missing?
options: An Internet Gateway route in that subnet
A 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway (in a public subnet)
A bigger instance type
An Elastic IP on the instance
questions.explanation: With only the local route, the subnet has zero internet path. Private instances get outbound via NAT: create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and add 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-... to the private route table. An IGW route would make the subnet public — not desired.

questions.question: CI needs cheap compute for interruptible test jobs. Which purchasing option fits best?
options: On-demand — simplest
Spot instances — up to ~90% cheaper, and job interruption is acceptable
3-year reserved instances
Dedicated hosts
questions.explanation: Spot sells spare capacity at deep discount with a 2-minute interruption notice — a perfect match for stateless, retryable CI workloads. Reserved/savings plans suit steady 24/7 baselines; dedicated hosts are for licensing/compliance.

questions.question: Write the AWS CLI command that shows which identity (account/ARN) your current credentials belong to.
questions.explanation: The 'whoami' of AWS. Run it before anything destructive — wrong-account incidents are legendary. It needs no permissions beyond being authenticated.

questions.question: Write the command to sync the local directory ./build to the bucket s3://acme-web (high-level CLI).
questions.explanation: s3 sync copies only new/changed files (like rsync) — the standard deploy step for static sites; add --delete to remove remote files that no longer exist locally.

questions.question: Why should subnets (and the resources in them) be spread across multiple Availability Zones?
options: Cross-AZ traffic is free
AZs are physically separate data centers; spreading across them survives a single-AZ failure
Each AZ has different instance prices
It's required for IPv6
questions.explanation: An AZ is one or more isolated data centers. ALB + Auto Scaling across ≥2 AZs is the baseline HA pattern; a single-AZ design turns an AWS zonal event into your outage. (Cross-AZ data transfer actually costs money — a tradeoff, not a reason.)

questions.question: What is EC2 user data?
options: Metadata about the instance owner
A script executed on first boot, used to bootstrap the instance (install packages, join clusters)
The instance's EBS snapshot
Per-user home directories
questions.explanation: User data runs via cloud-init on first boot (by default) — the standard hook for bootstrap: install agent, pull config, register with the fleet. For repeatable fleets, bake AMIs (Packer) and keep user data minimal.
